definition: Site Reliability Engineering — an operating discipline that manages reliability through measurable objectives, shared ownership, and deliberate change.
Service Level Objective — the target level of reliability a service commits to, expressed against a measurable indicator.
Service Level Indicator — the measurement used to evaluate an SLO, such as availability or request latency.
Service Level Agreement — a contractual reliability commitment, usually looser than the internal SLO.
Center for Enablement — the team that owns standards, onboarding, and enablement for the observability platform rather than owning each service.
Real User Monitoring — telemetry captured from actual user sessions in the browser or mobile app.
The Dynatrace agent installed on a host to collect infrastructure, process, service, and trace data automatically.
A vendor-neutral standard for generating and exporting traces, metrics, and logs; an alternative route to trace ingestion.
A Dynatrace construct that scopes which entities a group of users can see, used to align access with service ownership.
The detected map of hosts, processes, services, and their relationships, used for impact analysis.
Scheduled HTTP or browser tests that actively validate availability and response time for a critical journey.
The Dynatrace configuration that decides which problems generate a notification, and where that notification goes.
IT Service Management — the ticketing and incident tooling that alerts route into at handoff.
Mean Time To Resolve — the average elapsed time from detection to service restoration.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — a model for assigning ownership across roles.
Role-Based Access Control.
The criticality classification applied to the most business-critical services, driving coverage depth and validation rigour.
The Google SRE term for the acceptable amount of unreliability implied by an SLO (100% minus the SLO) — spent deliberately on release risk, and a signal to slow down once exhausted.
The Google SRE term for manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with the size of the estate rather than getting easier over time — the reason standardized guides like this one exist.
The four signals the Google SRE book recommends watching for any user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
Microsoft's set of five pillars — Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency — for evaluating architecture and platform decisions on Azure.

Independent research findings (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service) that measure software delivery speed and stability together, regardless of platform or vendor.
A Google SRE incident-review practice that assumes good intentions from everyone involved and focuses on fixing systems rather than assigning fault.
